title: Microporous MOF for simultaneous high thermodynamic and kinetic synergistic separation of propylene and propane

paper_content.abstract: Efficient separation of propylene from propane is a critical yet challenging industrial process. While rigid molecular sieves offer ideal selectivity, their narrow nanopores inherently constrain adsorption capacity and diffusion kinetics due to compromised thermodynamic-kinetic trade-offs. To address this, we report ZSTU-10, a molecular sieve constructed via structure-directing agents. Uniquely, ZSTU-10 features localized sieving gates for selective guest admission, expansive diffusion channels for rapid transport, and central pore cavities for high-capacity storage. This gate-channel-cavity architecture enables the precise exclusion of propane while facilitating the dense packing and fast diffusion of propylene, achieving simultaneous thermodynamic-kinetics optimization in molecular sieving. Static adsorption experiments demonstrate an exceptional propylene uptake (97.7 cm3 cm-3) at 298 K and 1 bar. Time-dependent uptake kinetics revealed a propylene diffusion coefficient (4.29 × 10-9 cm2 s-1) in ZSTU-10 surpassing benchmarks by two orders of magnitude. Dynamic breakthrough experiments demonstrate that ZSTU-10 produces high-purity propylene (99.1%) with a productivity of 37.5 L kg−1 in a single adsorption-desorption cycle.
paper_content.introduction:
Propylene is one of the most crucial olefins in the petrochemistry industry that serves as a primary feedstock for manufacturing various consumer products and chemicals1,2. Industrial propylene (C3H6) is mainly produced via steam cracking of naphtha or fluid catalytic cracking by hydrocarbons, with propane (C3H8) as a by-product3-5. The established industrial route to obtain high-purity C3H6 (> 99.5%) from C3H6/C3H8 mixtures relies on traditional thermal-driven cryogenic distillation, which is highly energy intensive separation due to the small volatility difference between the two molecules6-9. Therefore, it is imperative to develop alternative separation technologies with lower energy input and reduced capital cost. Porous materials including zeolites10-16, activated carbons17,18, and metal-organic frameworks (MOFs)19-21 have garnered considerable attention as non-thermal separation platforms, offering the potential to markedly reduce energy consumption relative to cryogenic distillation. However, conventional zeolites and activated carbons often face limitations in simultaneously achieving high selectivity, high working capacity, and fast mass transport for the challenging C3H6/C3H8 mixtures, owing to restricted pore-size tunability or broad pore-size distributions. In contrast, MOFs provide highly programmable pore environments and precisely engineerable adsorption sites, enabling rational design of molecular-sieving apertures and host–guest interactions, which has led to their extensively studied for olefin/alkane separation22-26.

MOFs utilizing thermodynamic separation principles exploit differences in adsorption affinity (e.g., via open metal sites) to achieve high equilibrium selectivity27,28. However, the strong host-guest interactions in such materials often necessitate substantial energy for regeneration. In contrast, kinetic separations rely on the differences in diffusion rates and typically feature tuned pore apertures and smooth surfaces to minimize transport resistance29-32. Consequently, this approach often suffers from weak host-guest confinement, failing to discriminate between closely related alkanes/alkenes and resulting in low selectivity. While molecular sieving MOFs achieve ultra-high selectivity as an extreme form of kinetic separation, enabled by precise size discrimination within small-sized guests33-36. Yet, they face an inherent structural paradox that the narrowly confined channels intrinsically limit adsorbate diffusion kinetics and reduce accessible adsorption capacity37,38. Furthermore, while elevated temperatures can enhance molecular mobility to mitigate diffusion constraints, they simultaneously reduce adsorption capacity due to exothermic thermodynamic effects. Resolving incompatibilities between pore size and pore shape of MOFs and the optimal operational conditions to achieve synergistic thermodynamic-kinetic separation remains a fundamental challenge39-42. To address these constraints, we develop a solvent-templated nanoconfinement strategy that precisely tailors MOF pore apertures (in the 3-5 Å regime) and optimizes process conditions (e.g., temperature) to achieve a thermodynamically-kinetically balanced separation. The resulting framework integrates localized molecular sieving gate to selective guest admission, interconnected auxiliary large channels that function as bridge-mediated guest diffusion pathways, and central cavity acting as high-capacity storage reservoirs. This gate-channel-cavity architecture cooperatively enhances diffusion kinetics, guest storage capacity, and host-guest binding affinities (Fig. 1).

Herein, using N-butyl alcohol/N-propyl alcohol /Isopropyl alcohol (n-BuOH/n-PrOH/i-PrOH) as solvent templates, we constructed three isoreticular ultra-microporous MOFs (denoted ZSTU-10, ZSTU-11, and ZSTU-12). These isostructural MOFs feature central pore cages radially connected to constricted gate apertures via diffusion channels, forming an interpenetrated three-dimensional (3D) channel system. Notably, the effective gate aperture of ZSTU-10 precisely interposes between the minimum cross-sections of C3H6 (3.8 × 4.1 Å2) and C3H8 (3.3 × 4.2 Å2), enabling molecular sieving via size exclusion. Gas adsorption analyses reveal a high volumetric C3H6 uptake (97.7 cm3 cm-3) and a notable combined C3H6/C3H8 equilibrium-kinetic selectivity of 2 × 103. The C3H6 diffusion coefficient (4.29 × 10-9 cm2 s-1) rivals benchmark ZU-609 material, while the pronounced C3H6/C3H8 diffusion-rate differentiation is attributed to the cooperative effect of the localized sieving gate and the short, low-resistance diffusion pathways. Dynamic breakthrough experiments reveal that ZSTU-10 is capable of obtaining high-purity C3H6 (99.1%) with a productivity of 37.5 L kg-1. Crystallography studies and neutron powder diffraction experiments confirm this unique framework of ZSTU-10 overcomes intrinsic constraints to achieve high adsorption capacity, rapid diffusion kinetics, and ideal host-guest interactions.
paper_content.results:
Synthesis and characterization
Colorless, rectangular prismatic crystals of ZSTU-10, ZSTU-11, and ZSTU-12 were synthesized via a solvothermal reaction involving zinc carbonate (ZnCO3), 1,2,4-1H-triazole (TRZ), and oxalic acid in a solvent mixture of water (H2O) and n-BuOH/n-PrOH/i-PrOH (Fig. 2a). Single-crystal X-ray diffraction (SCXRD) reveals that three isoreticular MOFs crystallize in the monoclinic P21/c space group, with symmetrical building blocks comprising Zn nodes and organic linkers arranged systematically (Supplementary Table 1). In all three structures, each pentahedral Zn center is coordinated by three nitrogen atoms from three distinct triazolate linkers and two oxygen atoms from a single oxalate ligand. The planar conjugation of triazoles facilitates their preferential coordination with Zn, forming two-dimensional 2D layered [Zn(TRZ)]n. These layers are subsequently pillared by oxalate units to form a three-dimensional (3D) framework with a dmc topology (Supplementary Fig. 1), which is isostructural to the benchmark CALF-20 framework known for its high stability43. The solvent-accessible voids for ZSTU-10, ZSTU-11 and ZSTU-12, as determined by the PLATON program, are 40.2%, 40.4% and 40.1%, respectively. The powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns of the as-synthesized samples match well with the simulated patterns, verifying their superior bulk phase purity and crystallinity (Supplementary Figs. 13-14). Notably, the PXRD patterns reveal a progressive shift of the peak for the (100) planes to lower 2θ values from ZSTU-10 to ZSTU-12. An in-depth examination confirmed that the template solvents induce subtle structural variations in bond angles and lengths. The quantitative ∠N-Zn-O angles are 164.68°, 164.80°, and 165.09°, while the angles of adjacent triazoles are 98.60°, 99.37° and 97.48° for ZSTU-10, ZSTU-11, and ZSTU-12, respectively (Fig. 2b-d and Supplementary Fig. 5). These geometric variations effectively modulate the gate apertures and channel cross-sections.

SCXRD analysis, visualized via Connolly surface, demonstrates that ZSTU-10 features a center nanocage interconnected with surrounding diffusion channels. It possesses an optimal sieving gate of 4.4 × 3.4 Å2 aligned with the crystallographic c axis (Fig. 2f), with an intermediate estimated cross-section area of 14.96 Å2, which is substantially larger than the minimum cross-section of C3H6 (13.86 Å2) yet smaller than that of C3H8 (15.58 Å2). By comparison, the gates in ZSTU-11 and ZSTU-12, with aperture dimensions of 4.9 × 3.1 Å2, and 4.6 × 2.9 Å2, either fails to recognize guests or blocks their entry (Supplementary Fig. 3-4). Since the gate aperture serves as the dominant geometric determinant for sieving selectivity, these structural differences suggest that ZSTU-10 exhibits a potential size-selective sieving effect on C3H6 and C3H8. Furthermore, the built-in large channels facilitate the rapid transport of guests into the central cavities, firmly locking them in place, which is crucial for prompting adsorbate diffusion and storage capacity.

ZSTU-10 possesses a sufficiently large cavity with dimensions of 8.5 × 6.3 × 6.5 Å3, interconnected on all sides by diffusion channels 4.7 × 3.0 Å2 (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Fig. 2). Such channel dimensions are sufficiently open to facilitate fast C3H6 diffusion, while the cage volume supports high packing density and thus high volumetric uptake. This comprehensive structural analysis suggests that ZSTU-10 possesses the optimal pore aperture and channel for C3 separation.

The structural robustness and phase identify of the ZSTU series were rigorously validated through complementary diffraction techniques and solvent-stability assays. To assess framework integrity upon activation, high-resolution neutron powder diffraction (NPD) was employed to characterize ZSTU-10/11/12. The NPD profiles of the as-synthesized and activated samples (ZSTU-10a/11a/12a) exhibit high structural uniformity with negligible deviation. (Supplementary Figs. 6-8 and Supplementary Figs. 11-12 and Supplementary Figs. 15-16). This structural invariance confirm that precise coordination environment and pore apertures are preserved without framework relaxation or collapse following the thorough evacuation of solvent molecules. Furthermore, systematic cross-solvent soaking experiments were conducted. Each material was immersed in the specific alcohols used for the synthesis of its isoreticular counterparts to evaluate potential phase transitions. The resulting PXRD patterns remained entirely unchanged (Supplementary Fig. 18), demonstrating that these frameworks do not undergo solvent-mediated interconversion. All ORTEP-style illustrations of ZSTU-10/11/12 were showed in the Supplementary Figs. 74-82. These results collectively confirm that the three isoreticular structures are independent stable states, whose specific pore metrics are inherent to the alcohol-templated assembly rather than reflecting meta-stable intermediates.

Porosity analyses and thermodynamic equilibrium adsorption
Thermogravimetric analysis indicates that all three MOFs maintain thermal stability up to 400 ℃. The initial weight loss steps correspond well with the evaporation temperatures of the respective solvent templates (Supplementary Fig. 10). Subsequently, the permanent porosity of ZSTU-10, ZSTU-11, and ZSTU-12 was evaluated by carbon dioxide (CO2) adsorption isotherms at 195 K and nitrogen (N2) adsorption isotherms at 77 K (Supplementary Figs. 22-24). Both ZSTU-10 and ZSTU-11 exhibit type-Ⅰ adsorption behaviors for CO2 and N2, whereas ZSTU-12 shows reversible type-Ⅰ CO2 adsorption isotherm but negligible N2 uptake at 77 K, which is attributed to the kinetic restriction of N2 diffusion through the narrower gate aperture in ZSTU-12. Based on N2 adsorption isotherms at 77 K, the Brunauer−Emmett−Teller (BET) surface areas of ZSTU-10 and ZSTU-11 were determined to be 406.2 m2 g-1 and 419.8 m2 g-1, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 25). The corresponding total pore volume were determined to be 0.18 cm3 g-1 and 0.249 cm3 g-1. For ZSTU-12, its microporous nature is confirmed by a CO2 uptake of 62.5 cm3 g-1 at 195 K, with an apparent surface area of 180 m2 g-1 and a total pore volume of 0.097 cm3 g-1. The pore size distribution for ZSTU-10, derived from the N2 adsorption isotherm at 77 K, is narrowly centered at 3.9 Å based on Horváth-Kawazoe (H-K) model, consistent with an ultra-microporous gate-dominated framework.

Motivated by their distinct gate apertures and large cavities, we investigated the adsorption performance of C3H6 and C3H8 in three MOFs. Single-component adsorption isotherms of C3H6 and C3H8 on ZSTU-10, ZSTU-11, and ZSTU-12 were collected at 298 K and 1 bar (Figs. 3a-b and Supplementary Fig. 39). ZSTU-11 demonstrates substantial adsorption capacity for both C3H6 and C3H8, which is attributed to its larger pore aperture that lacks size discrimination. In contrast, ZSTU-12 exhibited minimal adsorption for either gas across various temperatures, indicating kinetic blockage due to its constricted pores. Notably, ZSTU-10 exhibited a steep uptake of C3H6 and quickly reached equilibrium at low pressure, while completely excluded C3H8. ZSTU-10 achieved a significant C3H6 volumetric uptake of 92.5 cm3 cm-3 (57.0 cm3 g-1) at 0.1 bar and 298 K and reached a plateau at higher pressures. This exceptionally high low-pressure uptake is attributed to the synergistic effect of strong binding sites within the central cavity and rapid transport through diffusion channels, which was a common adsorption phenomenon observed in advanced adsorbents designed for high-affinity gas capture44. At 298 K and 1 bar, The C3H6 adsorption capacity reaches 97.7 cm3 cm-3 (60.9 cm3 g-1), reflecting its superior packing efficiency. The excellent C3H6 uptake of ZSTU-10 surpasses many benchmark sieving materials, such as ZU-609 (73.1/10.8 cm3 cm-3)45, Y-abtc (63/35 cm3 cm-3)37, Co-gallate (66.6/17.9 cm3 cm-3)38, JNU-3a (87.5/18.7 cm3 cm-3)35, KAUST-7 (61.9/10.1 cm3 cm-3)45-48 at 1 bar and 0.1 bar (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Table 11). Due to negligible adsorption of C3H8, ZSTU-10 possessed a significantly higher C3H6/C3H8 uptake ratio of 24.5, placing it among the top-performing materials (Supplementary Fig. 35)49. Remarkably, based on the absorbed C3H6 amount and the experimental pore volume, the packing density of C3H6 within ZSTU-10 is estimated to be 633 g L-1, which approaches the density of liquid C3H6 (608 g L-1) at its boiling point of 225 K and exceeds gaseous C3H6 at 298 K and 1 bar (1.707 g L-1) by a factor of approximately 370 times (Supplementary Fig. 34). These results indicate exceptionally efficient pore filling enabled by the optimized gate–channel–cavity architecture of ZSTU-10.

The ideal absorbed solution theory (IAST) was employed to evaluate the adsorption selectivity for an equimolar C3H6/C3H8 mixture, revealing an exceptionally high selectivity of 7 × 103 for ZSTU-10 (Supplementary Figs. 30-33 and Supplementary Table 11). Due to the ultralow capacity and the difficulty in achieving equilibrium for C3H8, fitting parameters of IAST selectivity for molecular sieving present certain uncertainties and errors that need to be acknowledged (Supplementary Tables 7-8). Encouraged by the outstanding low-pressure adsorption behaviors of ZSTU-10, Henry’s constant of C3H6 and C3H8, along with Henry’s selectivity were subsequently calculated based on the sorption isotherms across the entire pressure range with Langmuir fitting methods (Supplementary Fig. 36 and Supplementary Table 3)50-52. The Henry’s constant of C3H6 was estimated to be 174.3 mmol g-1 kPa-1 for ZSTU-10, and Henry’s selectivity was determined to be 124, considering the low Henry’s constant of C3H8 for ZSTU-10 (1.4 mmol g-1 kPa-1). This value far exceeds that of many C3H6-selective adsorbents, including DL-mal-MOF (5.86)42, and MAF-23-O (8.16)39, and Mg-MOF-74 (18.7)50 (Supplementary Fig. 37). Based on the adsorption isotherms at 313, 323 and 333 K, the isosteric heat of adsorption (Qst) of C3H6 on ZSTU-10 was calculated to be 45.5 kJ mol-1 at zero coverage using the virial method. For comparison, The Qst of C3H6 on ZSTU-11 is 37.3 kJ mol-1 according to C3H6 adsorption isotherms at 303, 313 and 323 K (Supplementary Figs. 26-29). The moderate adsorption enthalpy of ZSTU-10 indicates an energy-efficient regeneration process.

Adsorption kinetics
It is well established that the overall adsorption performance is governed not only by thermodynamic equilibrium factors, such as host-guest affinity and adsorption enthalpy, but also by the diffusion kinetics of guest molecules within the framework. An initial analysis of the structural features of the centered cage with diffusion channels in ZSTU-10 suggests that it is ideally configured to support the rapid kinetics of C3H6 molecules. To explore its kinetic advantage, time-dependent kinetic adsorption isotherms of ZSTU-10 and ZSTU-11 were measured from 283 K to 318 K at 1 bar (Supplementary Figs. 49-50). Remarkable differences in the diffusion coefficients of C3H6 and C3H8 were observed, with C3H6 diffusing much faster than C3H8, leading to an impressive kinetic selectivity of 286 for ZSTU-10 (Supplementary Fig. 38 and Supplementary Figs. 51-52 and Supplementary Tables 4-5). To further quantify this distinction, the calculated diffusion coefficient of C3H6 in ZSTU-10 was 4.29 × 10-9 cm2 s-1 at 298 K and 1 bar. This value is comparable to ZU-609 (1.36 × 10-9 cm2 s-1), and two orders of magnitude higher than other leading sieving materials such as Co-gallate (6.47 × 10-11 cm2 s-1), and KAUST-7 (9.49 × 10-11 cm2 s-1) (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Fig. 9 and Figs. 53-54 and Supplementary Table 6)53. By combining this superior kinetics adsorption with the aforementioned thermodynamic equilibrium performances, ZSTU-10 achieves a more standard equilibrium-kinetic combined selectivity, which is up to 2 × 103. Such a high selectivity significantly outperforms most benchmark MOFs, such as DL-mal-MOF (62.6)42, MAF-23-O (68.8)39, Ni(AIP)(PBPY) (48.3)54 (Supplementary Table 10)55.

In an unexpected finding, the static equilibrium adsorption displayed a pattern that deviated from conventional exothermic principles. As a result, pure-component adsorption/desorption isotherms were measured for C3H6 and C3H8 over a temperature range from 243 K to 333 K (Supplementary Figs. 40-48). With the increase of temperature, the results revealed a volcano-type trend for C3H6 in ZSTU-10. The C3H6 uptake initially rose from 60.2 cm3 cm-3 to 97.3 cm3 cm-3 and then decreased to 91.2 cm3 cm-3, reaching a maximum at 298 K (Fig. 3d). In contrast, C3H8 adsorption does not reach equilibrium under the same conditions and shows an apparent increase with temperature, consistent with kinetically limited uptake. To probe the origin of this behavior, single-crystal X-ray diffraction data and in situ variable-temperature PXRD were collected at different temperatures (Supplementary Fig. 17 and Supplementary Table 1). Both analyses indicate that the framework of ZSTU-10 remains essentially rigid across the examined temperatures, and the key geometric parameters of the sieving gate (4.4 × 3.4 Å2) and diffusion channel show no discernible changes, indicating that these factors were not rationale for effect on adsorption (Supplementary Figs. 55-57). Similar temperature-dependent anomalies have been reported by Fernandez. et al56 and Zhou. et al57, leading to the inference that lower temperatures diminish the kinetic energy of guest molecules, hindering their ability to surpass the aperture energy barrier despite favorable thermodynamics58,59. Consistent with this interpretation, time-dependent adsorption isotherms demonstrated that the enhanced intrinsic kinetic energy of guest with rising temperature yield faster diffusion coefficients (Supplementary Table 6). It is suggested that the optimal configuration of the pore gate and diffusion channel collectively establish an optimal operating window around 298 K, where transport limitations are sufficiently alleviated while adsorption affinity remains high, thereby enabling simultaneous high thermodynamic and kinetic separation of C3H6/C3H8.

Host-guest structure studies
To elucidate the adsorption mechanism and host-guest interactions of C3H6 and C3H8 in ZSTU-10, we performed Grand Canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) simulations at room temperature and 0.1 kPa, 10 kPa and 100 kPa, together with Dispersion-corrected density functional theory (DFT-D) calculations to evaluate the binding force of C3H6 molecules in ZSTU-10. At ambient temperature and 100 kPa, the density distribution maps indicate C3 molecules are preferentially located near the oxalate ligands of ZSTU-10, proving that gas molecules diffuse into the cavity parallel to the c-axis of the pore window. Compared to the C3H8 density, the simulated C3H6 density was significantly higher at 0.1 kPa. Moreover, with the pressure increases, a dense packing of C3H6 molecules exhibits minimal variation between 10 kPa and 100 kPa, consistent with the experimentally observe steep low-pressure uptake (Supplementary Fig. 58). Furthermore, GCMC simulations revealed that two C3H6 molecules were adsorbed in the central large cavity, which is consistent with the static adsorption data. DFT-D calculations were conducted to quantify the adsorbent-adsorbate binding energy in ZSTU-10 (Supplementary Fig. 59). Corroborating the GCMC results, C3H6 molecules in ZSTU-10 primarily anchor to the oxygen atoms of the oxalate ligands, forming strong C-H···O interactions (2.701-2.987 Å). Additional weaker C-H···O interactions at around 3.933 Å are formed with distal oxygen atoms. Along the b-axis direction, C3H6 molecules interact with the triazole linkers via hydrogen-bonding interactions of d(C3H6···TRZ) C-N···H at around 2.477-2.980 Å. The static binding energy of C3H6 at the binding sites was calculated to be 41.4 kJ mol-1, which is in good agreement with the experimental Qst value (45.5 kJ mol-1). In comparison, the static binding energy of C3H8 was only 13.2 kJ mol-1, revealing much weaker binding forces. As depicted in Supplementary Fig. 62, C3H6 molecules located in the middle of the pore cavity in ZSTU-11, forming multiple C-H···O interactions (2.792-3.536 Å) and intermolecular d(C3H6···TRZ) C-H···N (2.999-3.246 Å) interactions with the framework. The calculated static binding energy for C3H6 in ZSTU-11 is 42.4 kJ mol-1, while the static binding energy for C3H8 is 20.3 kJ mol-1, with the latter being higher than in ZSTU-10 (Supplementary Figs. 61-62). Moreover, electrostatic potentials (ESP) of the pore structure of ZSTU-10, ZSTU-11, and ZSTU-12 were also calculated by DFT-D calculations, and the differentiated framework energy was exhibited in Supplementary Figs. 63-65 (the corresponding energy order is ZSTU-11 > ZSTU-10 > ZSTU-12). The results reveal strong negative potentials near the oxygen atoms of oxalate ligands. Simulated results and calculated static binding energies are consistent with the experimental sorption phenomenon of ZSTU-10 and ZSTU-11.

To obtain direct structural insight into the adsorption behavior of ZSTU-10, high-resolution neutron powder diffraction (NPD) experiments were conducted to accurately establish the supramolecular binding forces between C3D6 molecules and the framework (Supplementary Fig. 11b). Two independent adsorption sites (site Ι and Ⅱ) of C3D6 molecules were identified within the pore cavity constructed by four oxalate and eight triazole ligands, as shown in Figs. 4a-b and Supplementary Fig. 60). The occupancy of two C3D6 adsorption sites was refined to be 0.133 and 0.364 at sites Ι and Ⅱ, respectively, indicating that each unit cell can accommodate two C3D6 molecules. This result corresponds to a volumetric uptake of 101.0 cm3 cm-3 (STP), which is in excellent agreement with the experimental uptake from the C3H6 isotherm (97.3 cm3 cm-3) at 298 K and 1 bar. As depicted in Fig. 4, site Ⅱ serves as the predominant sorption site and owns a higher occupancy, which was anchored by the surrounding oxalate ligands to form multiple C-D···O interactions (2.386-3.402 Å). Site Ι is located adjacent to the oxalate ligands and triazole ligands, binding to these ligands via C-D···N interactions (2.048-3.361 Å) and stronger C-D···O (2.222-3.501 Å) hydrogen bonds (Fig. 4c). In addition, a negligible framework deformation can be found when comparing the structure of activated ZSTU-10 with that of C3D6-loaded ZSTU-10, confirming the structural rigidity of ZSTU-10. These results demonstrate that the precise pore window and expansive cavity are prerequisites for achieving effective molecular sieving and high-density C3H6 packing, while the interconnected diffusion channels are essential for facilitating rapid guest transport.

Breakthrough experiments
Motivated by the superior separation capacity of ZSTU-10 in single-component adsorption/desorption performance, we further conducted binary C3H6/C3H8 (v/v=50/50) column breakthrough experiments, in which equimolar binary mixtures flowed over the sample bed of MOFs with different flow rates at 298 K (Supplementary Fig. 66). Dynamic breakthrough experiments revealed that both ZSTU-10 and ZSTU-11 are capable of separating C3H6 from an equimolar C3H6/C3H8 mixtures (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Fig. 71). However, the separation efficiency distinguishes the two materials. Notably, at a total flow rate of 3 mL min-1, the breakthrough curves for the equimolar C3H6/C3H8 mixture show that C3H8 elutes first, and the co-adsorption interval is short (4.2 min g-1). After the overlap ends, a clear time window is observed in which C3H6 is retained while C3H8 has already eluted, enabling a wide separation window with mass-normalized retention time of approximately 16.6 min g-1 for high-purity C3H6 collection (Fig. 5a). The dynamic C3H6 capacity of ZSTU-10 was calculated to be 2.76 mmol g-1 based on C3H6/C3H8 breakthrough adsorption curves, surpassing that of ZU-609 (1.64 mmol g-1)60, KAUST-7 (0.65 mmol g-1)37, Y-abtc (1.26 mmol g-1)37 and Co-gallate (0.98 mmol g-1)38 (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 67). At a higher flow rate of 5 mL min-1, ZSTU-10 maintains a limited co-adsorption interval (8.6 min g-1), whereas ZSTU-11 exhibits a substantially longer co-adsorption interval (15 min g-1) under comparable conditions (Supplementary Figs. 68 and 72). Besides, the retention time of C3H6/C3H8 for ZSTU-11 below the co-adsorption interval reveals the poor separation efficiency. The shorter overlap for ZSTU-10 indicates reduced co-elution and thus improved dynamic separation performance for equimolar C3H6/C3H8 mixtures. The excellent breakthrough performance of ZSTU-10 prompted us to explore C3H6 purity and productivity, the desorption experiments were conducted through helium gas sweeping (10 mL min-1) at 448 K (Supplementary Fig. 69). Correspondingly, the purity and productivity of the preferentially adsorbed C3H6 was 99.1% and 37.5 L kg-1 (Figs. 5e-f and Supplementary Fig. 70). These metrics exceed those of reported benchmark MOFs with sensational performance, such as for KAUST-7 (16.3 L kg-1, 90% purity )46 and Y-abtc (1.3 L kg-1, 90% purity)37 (Supplementary Table 9). Five consecutive breakthrough adsorption/desorption measurements for an equimolar C3H6/C3H8 mixture were carried out at the flow rate of 5 mL min-1. The results revealed consistent retention times, no obvious loss of capacity, and a sustained C3H6 dynamic capture at around 3.7 mmol g-1 (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Fig. 68), confirming the excellent regenerability and cycling stability of ZSTU-10. Overall, these dynamic results demonstrate the practical potential of ZSTU-10 for C3H6/C3H8 separation. Because C3H8 adsorption is strongly suppressed by molecular sieving, regeneration primarily involves desorbing C3H6 from the high-affinity sites, which can reduce unnecessary energy expenditure associated with co-adsorbed impurities.

Given the demanding conditions prevalent in practical industrial production, we investigated the stability of ZSTU-10 under a range of relevant environments. The synthesized sample was exposed to air for 15 d and immersed in water for a week. The PXRD patterns indicate that ZSTU-10 can maintain substantial structural integrity without phase change or loss of crystallinity. Stable adsorption capacities of C3H6 for ZSTU-10 can be preserved after treatment with water at different time intervals (Supplementary Fig. 19). Furthermore, this material was soaked in different chemical environments for a week, such as organic solvents (DMF, MeOH, EtOH, CH2Cl2, ACN and acetone) and acid and alkaline solutions (pH = 2, 4, 10, 12). In all cases, the samples exhibited PXRD patterns identical to the simulated one, demonstrating exceptional chemical stability (Supplementary Figs. 20-21). Five consecutive single-component adsorption-desorption isotherms were conducted at 298 K and 1 bar, which consistently showed high levels of C3H6 adsorption capacity on ZSTU-10 (Fig. 5g and Supplementary Fig. 72). Additionally, the synthesis of ZSTU-10 uses inexpensive, readily available raw materials and demonstrates potential for scalability. Combined the advantages of good stability, low production cost, and the ability to simultaneously exclude C3H8 while efficiently adsorbing C3H6 renders ZSTU-10 a promising candidate for industrial application.
paper_content.methods:
Synthesis of ZSTU-10
ZnCO3 (0.627 g, 5 mmol), H2C2O4 (0.45 g, 5 mmol), and 1,2,4-triazole (TRZ, 1.727 g, 25 mmol) were added to the mixture of H2O (15 mL) and N-butyl alcohol (n-BuOH) (15 mL) in a 100 mL Teflon-lined reaction vessel. The mixed solution was stirred for an hour and reacted in an oven at 453 K for three days. After cooling to room temperature naturally, the resulting colorless crystals were collected by filtration and washed thoroughly with methanol. Finally, the product was dried in air overnight. To assess the potential for scale-up, we optimized the synthesis conditions. We confirmed that ZSTU-10 can be synthesized with high purity and crystallinity using a reduced molar ratio of 1:1:5, significantly lowering ligand consumption. Based on this optimized ratio and laboratory reagent prices, the estimated raw material cost is approximately $50.1 kg-1 (Supplementary Fig. 73), which serves as a promising baseline for future industrial economic evaluation.

Synthesis of ZSTU-11 and ZSTU-12
ZSTU-11 and ZSTU-12 were synthesized following the same procedure as ZSTU-10, except that n-BuOH was replaced by n-propyl alcohol (n-PrOH) or Isopropyl alcohol (i-PrOH), respectively.

Single-component sorption experiments
Prior to gas adsorption tests, approximately 200 mg of samples in the sample cell were activated under a dynamic vacuum at 423 K overnight to remove the guest molecules until the pressure stabilized. After each single-adsorption measurement, the sample cell was degassed at 333 K under vacuum for 0.5 h. C3H6 and C3H8 adsorption isotherms were collected from 243 K to 333 K on an automatic volumetric adsorption instrument (Micromeritics 3-Flex analyzer, 3-Flex Version 5.02). For each pressure point, an equilibrium time of 6 min was applied. Data were recorded only after a stability criterion was met: the system pressure changed by less than 0.1% over a consecutive 2 min period. The experimental adsorption-desorption temperatures were controlled by the ice bath (273 K) and a constant water bath (298 K). The Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) specific surface areas were analyzed using nitrogen adsorption isotherms at 77 K. The 195 K CO2 was performed in the mixtures of dry ice and acetone. The low temperatures from 243 K to 263 K were controlled by the mixtures of dry ice, ethanol, and ethylene glycol. The data visualization uses OriginPro 2024.

Dynamic breakthrough experiments
Fixed bed breakthrough experiments were carried out in a packed stainless steel column (10 mm × 12 cm) at 298 K and 1 bar. The breakthrough column was filled with activated samples (3.6 g) at ambient conditions. A stream of Argon was introduced into the column to purge the adsorbents for 15 h at 423 K in a temperature controller of the thermostat before the breakthrough experiments. The total inlet flow rate was controlled by calibrated mass flow controllers (MFCs) and was kept constant throughout each breakthrough experiment. The breakthrough column experiments were conducted using the gas mixture of C3H6/C3H8 (v/v, 50/50) with a stable flow rate of 5 mL min-1 at 298 K, and the outgas of the column was monitored by a gas chromatograph (GC-2014C Shimadzu) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector for continuous gas analysis. When both C3H6 and C3H8 reached equilibrium, the desorption experiments were conducted through high-purity Ar (99.999%) with a flow rate of 10 mL min-1 at 298 K, and then heated up to 448 K to sweep. Five consecutive breakthrough adsorption–desorption cycles were performed to evaluate the cycling stability of ZSTU-10.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This work by Wang et al. reported three isoreticular ultramicroporous metal-organic frameworks (ZSTU-10, ZSTU-11, and
ZSTU-12) for the selective molecular sieving of C3H6 from binary C3H6/C3H8 mixtures. Their results revealed that n-
butanol, as structure-directing agents constructed optimal sieving gates that efficiently distinguished C3H6 while fully
excluding C3H8. Simultaneously, it shaped the diffusion channels and central pore cavities to achieve exceptional C3H6
uptake and a thermodynamic-kinetics equilibrium separation. Detailed gas adsorption isotherms, dynamic breakthrough
experiments and gas loaded single-crystal X-ray diffraction fully substantiated these findings. Moreover, the authors
inverstigated these MOFs under different conditions and comfirmed its viability and effectiveness. Therefore, the overall
novelty of this work is sufficient and the olefin/alkane separation is very pivotal in industry. I can recommend this for
publication in Nature Communication after revisions. Here are some sepcific comments.
1. Based on its molecular structure and static adsorption isotherms, ZSTU-10 exhibits exceptionally high C3H6/C3H8
selectivity. What advantages does it offer compared to previously reported sieving materials?
2. The dmc topology reported in this work is not commoly encountered, and a more comprehensive literature-based
discussion of the topological configuration of ZSTU-10 would greatly help the article readers.
3. The author presents adsorption data in units of cm3 cm-3 (volumetric) rather than the conventional units of cm3 g-1 and
mmol g-1 (gravimetric). Colud the authors clarify the necessity for using volumetric adsorption and discuss its advantages in
this specific context compared to gravimetric units?
4. In the synthesis and characterization section, there is an inconsistency between the manuscript and the supplementary
information regarding the reported cavity size. The manuscirpt states the dimension as 8.5 × 6.3 × 6.5 Å3, whereas the
supporting information lists it as 8.5 × 6.0 × 6.2 Å3, so this mistake should be corrected for consistency.
5. In Fig. 3d, the C3H6/C3H8 uptake ratio is not presemt in the figure; instead, the data likely represent the C3H6 uptake at
0.1 bar from 243 K to 333 K.
6. In Supplementary Figure 72, the components in the breakthrough curves are mislabeled, because the more strongly
adsorbed component of C3H6 should not be eluted first.
7. The manuscript conatins several grammatical and typographical erroes that require attention. For example:
Page 7, the term “Qst” should be defined upon its first introduction, which occurs in the preceding sentence.
Page 9, the multiple C-H···O interactions in ZSTU-11 is given as 2.793-3.536 Å but should be corrected to 2.792-3.536 Å.
In Fig. 5d, the chemical formulas “C3H6” and “C3H8” should be formatted with subscripts as “C3H6” and “C3H8”.
8. The raw materials used by the author are very cheap. Has large-scale synthesis and economic evaluation been
conducted? This is very meaningful for practical applications.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors have synthesized a MOF series, featuring central pore cages with sieving gates apertures connected to fast
diffusion channels, using alcohol structure directing agents. The obtained ZSTU-10 MOF achieved a good separation of
propylene from propane via a thermodynamic-kinetics equilibrium optimization in molecular sieving. The study is
meaningful, addressing the key bottleneck of thermodynamic-kinetic trade-off. And the resultant propylene uptake and
diffusion coefficient have exceeded those of the MOFs with similar cavity-channel microstructures. The manuscript is well
written, the experimental evidences are self-consistent. But still, some key questions need to be answered before it is
publication. The detailed comments are listed as below.
1. The authors addressed the structure-directing agents of the three alcohols to template the featured pore structures of
ZSTU-10, 11 and 12, they only provided the final results of the bond angles and lengths. There was a lack of a discussion of
their roles on the subtle differences of the isoreticular micropores shown in Figure 1a. Besides, have all the solvent
molecules been removed from the cavities to conduct the subsequent characterizations? Will the pore apertures maintain
after thoroughly removing all the water and alcohol solvent molecules at elevated temperatures? It is surprising that ZSTU-
12 displayed a negligible N2 uptake compared to ZSTU-10 and 11. Overall, the authors need to carefully validate whether
the three isoreticular structures are de facto one accompanied with two intermediate state structures.
2. The C3H6 uptake for ZSTU-10 at 0.1 bar has approached to the saturated adsorption capacity (97.7 cm3 cm-3) at 1 bar.
The value has far surpassed other MOF sorption performances. Please present a discussion on this phenomenon.
3. The 50/50 propylene/propane co-adsorption analysis should be supplemented.
4. There are many clerical errors. For example, there is no Fig. 3i in the main text, it should be Fig. 3f.
5. Fig. 5d, why is there a peak signal for C3H6 desorption? And how does the ZSTU perform for a consecutive breakthrough
cycles, like four or five times. Please present the breakthrough curves.

(1) For IAST Calculations (Supplementary Note 1): The Dual-Site Langmuir-
Freundlich (DSLF) model was selected because it provides a highly accurate
mathematical fit over the entire pressure range (from 0 to 1 bar). IAST calculations are
sensitive to the fitting precision, especially for isotherms with heterogeneity or
inflection points. The DSLF model, with its additional parameters, captures these
features better than a simple Langmuir model, ensuring reliable mixture selectivity
predictions.
(2) For Henry’s Constants (Supplementary Note 3): The Langmuir model was
specifically applied to fit the low-pressure region (infinite dilution limit). In this regime,
adsorption behavior is dominated by adsorbent-adsorbate interactions rather than
adsorbate-adsorbate interactions. The Langmuir equation allows for the direct and
robust extraction of the Henry’s constant from the initial slope (affinity parameter b),
avoiding the potential over-parameterization issues of DSLF in the linear region.

avoid confusion.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Efficient separation of propylene from propane is a critical yet challenging industrial process. While rigid molecular sieves offer ideal selectivity, their narrow nanopores inherently constrain adsorption capacity and diffusion kinetics due to compromised thermodynamic-kinetic trade-offs. To address this, we report ZSTU-10, a molecular sieve constructed via structure-directing agents. Uniquely, ZSTU-10 features localized sieving gates for selective guest admission, expansive diffusion channels for rapid transport, and central pore cavities for high-capacity storage. This gate-channel-cavity architecture enables the precise exclusion of propane while facilitating the dense packing and fast diffusion of propylene, achieving simultaneous thermodynamic-kinetics optimization in molecular sieving. Static adsorption experiments demonstrate an exceptional propylene uptake (97.7 cm3 cm-3) at 298 K and 1 bar. Time-dependent uptake kinetics revealed a propylene diffusion coefficient (4.29 × 10-9 cm2 s-1) in ZSTU-10 surpassing benchmarks by two orders of magnitude. Dynamic breakthrough experiments demonstrate that ZSTU-10 produces high-purity propylene (99.1%) with a productivity of 37.5 L kg−1 in a single adsorption-desorption cycle.

---

## Introduction

Propylene is one of the most crucial olefins in the petrochemistry industry that serves as a primary feedstock for manufacturing various consumer products and chemicals1,2. Industrial propylene (C3H6) is mainly produced via steam cracking of naphtha or fluid catalytic cracking by hydrocarbons, with propane (C3H8) as a by-product3-5. The established industrial route to obtain high-purity C3H6 (> 99.5%) from C3H6/C3H8 mixtures relies on traditional thermal-driven cryogenic distillation, which is highly energy intensive separation due to the small volatility difference between the two molecules6-9. Therefore, it is imperative to develop alternative separation technologies with lower energy input and reduced capital cost. Porous materials including zeolites10-16, activated carbons17,18, and metal-organic frameworks (MOFs)19-21 have garnered considerable attention as non-thermal separation platforms, offering the potential to markedly reduce energy consumption relative to cryogenic distillation. However, conventional zeolites and activated carbons often face limitations in simultaneously achieving high selectivity, high working capacity, and fast mass transport for the challenging C3H6/C3H8 mixtures, owing to restricted pore-size tunability or broad pore-size distributions. In contrast, MOFs provide highly programmable pore environments and precisely engineerable adsorption sites, enabling rational design of molecular-sieving apertures and host–guest interactions, which has led to their extensively studied for olefin/alkane separation22-26.

MOFs utilizing thermodynamic separation principles exploit differences in adsorption affinity (e.g., via open metal sites) to achieve high equilibrium selectivity27,28. However, the strong host-guest interactions in such materials often necessitate substantial energy for regeneration. In contrast, kinetic separations rely on the differences in diffusion rates and typically feature tuned pore apertures and smooth surfaces to minimize transport resistance29-32. Consequently, this approach often suffers from weak host-guest confinement, failing to discriminate between closely related alkanes/alkenes and resulting in low selectivity. While molecular sieving MOFs achieve ultra-high selectivity as an extreme form of kinetic separation, enabled by precise size discrimination within small-sized guests33-36. Yet, they face an inherent structural paradox that the narrowly confined channels intrinsically limit adsorbate diffusion kinetics and reduce accessible adsorption capacity37,38. Furthermore, while elevated temperatures can enhance molecular mobility to mitigate diffusion constraints, they simultaneously reduce adsorption capacity due to exothermic thermodynamic effects. Resolving incompatibilities between pore size and pore shape of MOFs and the optimal operational conditions to achieve synergistic thermodynamic-kinetic separation remains a fundamental challenge39-42. To address these constraints, we develop a solvent-templated nanoconfinement strategy that precisely tailors MOF pore apertures (in the 3-5 Å regime) and optimizes process conditions (e.g., temperature) to achieve a thermodynamically-kinetically balanced separation. The resulting framework integrates localized molecular sieving gate to selective guest admission, interconnected auxiliary large channels that function as bridge-mediated guest diffusion pathways, and central cavity acting as high-capacity storage reservoirs. This gate-channel-cavity architecture cooperatively enhances diffusion kinetics, guest storage capacity, and host-guest binding affinities (Fig. 1).

Herein, using N-butyl alcohol/N-propyl alcohol /Isopropyl alcohol (n-BuOH/n-PrOH/i-PrOH) as solvent templates, we constructed three isoreticular ultra-microporous MOFs (denoted ZSTU-10, ZSTU-11, and ZSTU-12). These isostructural MOFs feature central pore cages radially connected to constricted gate apertures via diffusion channels, forming an interpenetrated three-dimensional (3D) channel system. Notably, the effective gate aperture of ZSTU-10 precisely interposes between the minimum cross-sections of C3H6 (3.8 × 4.1 Å2) and C3H8 (3.3 × 4.2 Å2), enabling molecular sieving via size exclusion. Gas adsorption analyses reveal a high volumetric C3H6 uptake (97.7 cm3 cm-3) and a notable combined C3H6/C3H8 equilibrium-kinetic selectivity of 2 × 103. The C3H6 diffusion coefficient (4.29 × 10-9 cm2 s-1) rivals benchmark ZU-609 material, while the pronounced C3H6/C3H8 diffusion-rate differentiation is attributed to the cooperative effect of the localized sieving gate and the short, low-resistance diffusion pathways. Dynamic breakthrough experiments reveal that ZSTU-10 is capable of obtaining high-purity C3H6 (99.1%) with a productivity of 37.5 L kg-1. Crystallography studies and neutron powder diffraction experiments confirm this unique framework of ZSTU-10 overcomes intrinsic constraints to achieve high adsorption capacity, rapid diffusion kinetics, and ideal host-guest interactions.

---

## Results

Synthesis and characterization
Colorless, rectangular prismatic crystals of ZSTU-10, ZSTU-11, and ZSTU-12 were synthesized via a solvothermal reaction involving zinc carbonate (ZnCO3), 1,2,4-1H-triazole (TRZ), and oxalic acid in a solvent mixture of water (H2O) and n-BuOH/n-PrOH/i-PrOH (Fig. 2a). Single-crystal X-ray diffraction (SCXRD) reveals that three isoreticular MOFs crystallize in the monoclinic P21/c space group, with symmetrical building blocks comprising Zn nodes and organic linkers arranged systematically (Supplementary Table 1). In all three structures, each pentahedral Zn center is coordinated by three nitrogen atoms from three distinct triazolate linkers and two oxygen atoms from a single oxalate ligand. The planar conjugation of triazoles facilitates their preferential coordination with Zn, forming two-dimensional 2D layered [Zn(TRZ)]n. These layers are subsequently pillared by oxalate units to form a three-dimensional (3D) framework with a dmc topology (Supplementary Fig. 1), which is isostructural to the benchmark CALF-20 framework known for its high stability43. The solvent-accessible voids for ZSTU-10, ZSTU-11 and ZSTU-12, as determined by the PLATON program, are 40.2%, 40.4% and 40.1%, respectively. The powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns of the as-synthesized samples match well with the simulated patterns, verifying their superior bulk phase purity and crystallinity (Supplementary Figs. 13-14). Notably, the PXRD patterns reveal a progressive shift of the peak for the (100) planes to lower 2θ values from ZSTU-10 to ZSTU-12. An in-depth examination confirmed that the template solvents induce subtle structural variations in bond angles and lengths. The quantitative ∠N-Zn-O angles are 164.68°, 164.80°, and 165.09°, while the angles of adjacent triazoles are 98.60°, 99.37° and 97.48° for ZSTU-10, ZSTU-11, and ZSTU-12, respectively (Fig. 2b-d and Supplementary Fig. 5). These geometric variations effectively modulate the gate apertures and channel cross-sections.

SCXRD analysis, visualized via Connolly surface, demonstrates that ZSTU-10 features a center nanocage interconnected with surrounding diffusion channels. It possesses an optimal sieving gate of 4.4 × 3.4 Å2 aligned with the crystallographic c axis (Fig. 2f), with an intermediate estimated cross-section area of 14.96 Å2, which is substantially larger than the minimum cross-section of C3H6 (13.86 Å2) yet smaller than that of C3H8 (15.58 Å2). By comparison, the gates in ZSTU-11 and ZSTU-12, with aperture dimensions of 4.9 × 3.1 Å2, and 4.6 × 2.9 Å2, either fails to recognize guests or blocks their entry (Supplementary Fig. 3-4). Since the gate aperture serves as the dominant geometric determinant for sieving selectivity, these structural differences suggest that ZSTU-10 exhibits a potential size-selective sieving effect on C3H6 and C3H8. Furthermore, the built-in large channels facilitate the rapid transport of guests into the central cavities, firmly locking them in place, which is crucial for prompting adsorbate diffusion and storage capacity.

ZSTU-10 possesses a sufficiently large cavity with dimensions of 8.5 × 6.3 × 6.5 Å3, interconnected on all sides by diffusion channels 4.7 × 3.0 Å2 (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Fig. 2). Such channel dimensions are sufficiently open to facilitate fast C3H6 diffusion, while the cage volume supports high packing density and thus high volumetric uptake. This comprehensive structural analysis suggests that ZSTU-10 possesses the optimal pore aperture and channel for C3 separation.

The structural robustness and phase identify of the ZSTU series were rigorously validated through complementary diffraction techniques and solvent-stability assays. To assess framework integrity upon activation, high-resolution neutron powder diffraction (NPD) was employed to characterize ZSTU-10/11/12. The NPD profiles of the as-synthesized and activated samples (ZSTU-10a/11a/12a) exhibit high structural uniformity with negligible deviation. (Supplementary Figs. 6-8 and Supplementary Figs. 11-12 and Supplementary Figs. 15-16). This structural invariance confirm that precise coordination environment and pore apertures are preserved without framework relaxation or collapse following the thorough evacuation of solvent molecules. Furthermore, systematic cross-solvent soaking experiments were conducted. Each material was immersed in the specific alcohols used for the synthesis of its isoreticular counterparts to evaluate potential phase transitions. The resulting PXRD patterns remained entirely unchanged (Supplementary Fig. 18), demonstrating that these frameworks do not undergo solvent-mediated interconversion. All ORTEP-style illustrations of ZSTU-10/11/12 were showed in the Supplementary Figs. 74-82. These results collectively confirm that the three isoreticular structures are independent stable states, whose specific pore metrics are inherent to the alcohol-templated assembly rather than reflecting meta-stable intermediates.

Porosity analyses and thermodynamic equilibrium adsorption
Thermogravimetric analysis indicates that all three MOFs maintain thermal stability up to 400 ℃. The initial weight loss steps correspond well with the evaporation temperatures of the respective solvent templates (Supplementary Fig. 10). Subsequently, the permanent porosity of ZSTU-10, ZSTU-11, and ZSTU-12 was evaluated by carbon dioxide (CO2) adsorption isotherms at 195 K and nitrogen (N2) adsorption isotherms at 77 K (Supplementary Figs. 22-24). Both ZSTU-10 and ZSTU-11 exhibit type-Ⅰ adsorption behaviors for CO2 and N2, whereas ZSTU-12 shows reversible type-Ⅰ CO2 adsorption isotherm but negligible N2 uptake at 77 K, which is attributed to the kinetic restriction of N2 diffusion through the narrower gate aperture in ZSTU-12. Based on N2 adsorption isotherms at 77 K, the Brunauer−Emmett−Teller (BET) surface areas of ZSTU-10 and ZSTU-11 were determined to be 406.2 m2 g-1 and 419.8 m2 g-1, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 25). The corresponding total pore volume were determined to be 0.18 cm3 g-1 and 0.249 cm3 g-1. For ZSTU-12, its microporous nature is confirmed by a CO2 uptake of 62.5 cm3 g-1 at 195 K, with an apparent surface area of 180 m2 g-1 and a total pore volume of 0.097 cm3 g-1. The pore size distribution for ZSTU-10, derived from the N2 adsorption isotherm at 77 K, is narrowly centered at 3.9 Å based on Horváth-Kawazoe (H-K) model, consistent with an ultra-microporous gate-dominated framework.

Motivated by their distinct gate apertures and large cavities, we investigated the adsorption performance of C3H6 and C3H8 in three MOFs. Single-component adsorption isotherms of C3H6 and C3H8 on ZSTU-10, ZSTU-11, and ZSTU-12 were collected at 298 K and 1 bar (Figs. 3a-b and Supplementary Fig. 39). ZSTU-11 demonstrates substantial adsorption capacity for both C3H6 and C3H8, which is attributed to its larger pore aperture that lacks size discrimination. In contrast, ZSTU-12 exhibited minimal adsorption for either gas across various temperatures, indicating kinetic blockage due to its constricted pores. Notably, ZSTU-10 exhibited a steep uptake of C3H6 and quickly reached equilibrium at low pressure, while completely excluded C3H8. ZSTU-10 achieved a significant C3H6 volumetric uptake of 92.5 cm3 cm-3 (57.0 cm3 g-1) at 0.1 bar and 298 K and reached a plateau at higher pressures. This exceptionally high low-pressure uptake is attributed to the synergistic effect of strong binding sites within the central cavity and rapid transport through diffusion channels, which was a common adsorption phenomenon observed in advanced adsorbents designed for high-affinity gas capture44. At 298 K and 1 bar, The C3H6 adsorption capacity reaches 97.7 cm3 cm-3 (60.9 cm3 g-1), reflecting its superior packing efficiency. The excellent C3H6 uptake of ZSTU-10 surpasses many benchmark sieving materials, such as ZU-609 (73.1/10.8 cm3 cm-3)45, Y-abtc (63/35 cm3 cm-3)37, Co-gallate (66.6/17.9 cm3 cm-3)38, JNU-3a (87.5/18.7 cm3 cm-3)35, KAUST-7 (61.9/10.1 cm3 cm-3)45-48 at 1 bar and 0.1 bar (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Table 11). Due to negligible adsorption of C3H8, ZSTU-10 possessed a significantly higher C3H6/C3H8 uptake ratio of 24.5, placing it among the top-performing materials (Supplementary Fig. 35)49. Remarkably, based on the absorbed C3H6 amount and the experimental pore volume, the packing density of C3H6 within ZSTU-10 is estimated to be 633 g L-1, which approaches the density of liquid C3H6 (608 g L-1) at its boiling point of 225 K and exceeds gaseous C3H6 at 298 K and 1 bar (1.707 g L-1) by a factor of approximately 370 times (Supplementary Fig. 34). These results indicate exceptionally efficient pore filling enabled by the optimized gate–channel–cavity architecture of ZSTU-10.

The ideal absorbed solution theory (IAST) was employed to evaluate the adsorption selectivity for an equimolar C3H6/C3H8 mixture, revealing an exceptionally high selectivity of 7 × 103 for ZSTU-10 (Supplementary Figs. 30-33 and Supplementary Table 11). Due to the ultralow capacity and the difficulty in achieving equilibrium for C3H8, fitting parameters of IAST selectivity for molecular sieving present certain uncertainties and errors that need to be acknowledged (Supplementary Tables 7-8). Encouraged by the outstanding low-pressure adsorption behaviors of ZSTU-10, Henry’s constant of C3H6 and C3H8, along with Henry’s selectivity were subsequently calculated based on the sorption isotherms across the entire pressure range with Langmuir fitting methods (Supplementary Fig. 36 and Supplementary Table 3)50-52. The Henry’s constant of C3H6 was estimated to be 174.3 mmol g-1 kPa-1 for ZSTU-10, and Henry’s selectivity was determined to be 124, considering the low Henry’s constant of C3H8 for ZSTU-10 (1.4 mmol g-1 kPa-1). This value far exceeds that of many C3H6-selective adsorbents, including DL-mal-MOF (5.86)42, and MAF-23-O (8.16)39, and Mg-MOF-74 (18.7)50 (Supplementary Fig. 37). Based on the adsorption isotherms at 313, 323 and 333 K, the isosteric heat of adsorption (Qst) of C3H6 on ZSTU-10 was calculated to be 45.5 kJ mol-1 at zero coverage using the virial method. For comparison, The Qst of C3H6 on ZSTU-11 is 37.3 kJ mol-1 according to C3H6 adsorption isotherms at 303, 313 and 323 K (Supplementary Figs. 26-29). The moderate adsorption enthalpy of ZSTU-10 indicates an energy-efficient regeneration process.

Adsorption kinetics
It is well established that the overall adsorption performance is governed not only by thermodynamic equilibrium factors, such as host-guest affinity and adsorption enthalpy, but also by the diffusion kinetics of guest molecules within the framework. An initial analysis of the structural features of the centered cage with diffusion channels in ZSTU-10 suggests that it is ideally configured to support the rapid kinetics of C3H6 molecules. To explore its kinetic advantage, time-dependent kinetic adsorption isotherms of ZSTU-10 and ZSTU-11 were measured from 283 K to 318 K at 1 bar (Supplementary Figs. 49-50). Remarkable differences in the diffusion coefficients of C3H6 and C3H8 were observed, with C3H6 diffusing much faster than C3H8, leading to an impressive kinetic selectivity of 286 for ZSTU-10 (Supplementary Fig. 38 and Supplementary Figs. 51-52 and Supplementary Tables 4-5). To further quantify this distinction, the calculated diffusion coefficient of C3H6 in ZSTU-10 was 4.29 × 10-9 cm2 s-1 at 298 K and 1 bar. This value is comparable to ZU-609 (1.36 × 10-9 cm2 s-1), and two orders of magnitude higher than other leading sieving materials such as Co-gallate (6.47 × 10-11 cm2 s-1), and KAUST-7 (9.49 × 10-11 cm2 s-1) (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Fig. 9 and Figs. 53-54 and Supplementary Table 6)53. By combining this superior kinetics adsorption with the aforementioned thermodynamic equilibrium performances, ZSTU-10 achieves a more standard equilibrium-kinetic combined selectivity, which is up to 2 × 103. Such a high selectivity significantly outperforms most benchmark MOFs, such as DL-mal-MOF (62.6)42, MAF-23-O (68.8)39, Ni(AIP)(PBPY) (48.3)54 (Supplementary Table 10)55.

In an unexpected finding, the static equilibrium adsorption displayed a pattern that deviated from conventional exothermic principles. As a result, pure-component adsorption/desorption isotherms were measured for C3H6 and C3H8 over a temperature range from 243 K to 333 K (Supplementary Figs. 40-48). With the increase of temperature, the results revealed a volcano-type trend for C3H6 in ZSTU-10. The C3H6 uptake initially rose from 60.2 cm3 cm-3 to 97.3 cm3 cm-3 and then decreased to 91.2 cm3 cm-3, reaching a maximum at 298 K (Fig. 3d). In contrast, C3H8 adsorption does not reach equilibrium under the same conditions and shows an apparent increase with temperature, consistent with kinetically limited uptake. To probe the origin of this behavior, single-crystal X-ray diffraction data and in situ variable-temperature PXRD were collected at different temperatures (Supplementary Fig. 17 and Supplementary Table 1). Both analyses indicate that the framework of ZSTU-10 remains essentially rigid across the examined temperatures, and the key geometric parameters of the sieving gate (4.4 × 3.4 Å2) and diffusion channel show no discernible changes, indicating that these factors were not rationale for effect on adsorption (Supplementary Figs. 55-57). Similar temperature-dependent anomalies have been reported by Fernandez. et al56 and Zhou. et al57, leading to the inference that lower temperatures diminish the kinetic energy of guest molecules, hindering their ability to surpass the aperture energy barrier despite favorable thermodynamics58,59. Consistent with this interpretation, time-dependent adsorption isotherms demonstrated that the enhanced intrinsic kinetic energy of guest with rising temperature yield faster diffusion coefficients (Supplementary Table 6). It is suggested that the optimal configuration of the pore gate and diffusion channel collectively establish an optimal operating window around 298 K, where transport limitations are sufficiently alleviated while adsorption affinity remains high, thereby enabling simultaneous high thermodynamic and kinetic separation of C3H6/C3H8.

Host-guest structure studies
To elucidate the adsorption mechanism and host-guest interactions of C3H6 and C3H8 in ZSTU-10, we performed Grand Canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) simulations at room temperature and 0.1 kPa, 10 kPa and 100 kPa, together with Dispersion-corrected density functional theory (DFT-D) calculations to evaluate the binding force of C3H6 molecules in ZSTU-10. At ambient temperature and 100 kPa, the density distribution maps indicate C3 molecules are preferentially located near the oxalate ligands of ZSTU-10, proving that gas molecules diffuse into the cavity parallel to the c-axis of the pore window. Compared to the C3H8 density, the simulated C3H6 density was significantly higher at 0.1 kPa. Moreover, with the pressure increases, a dense packing of C3H6 molecules exhibits minimal variation between 10 kPa and 100 kPa, consistent with the experimentally observe steep low-pressure uptake (Supplementary Fig. 58). Furthermore, GCMC simulations revealed that two C3H6 molecules were adsorbed in the central large cavity, which is consistent with the static adsorption data. DFT-D calculations were conducted to quantify the adsorbent-adsorbate binding energy in ZSTU-10 (Supplementary Fig. 59). Corroborating the GCMC results, C3H6 molecules in ZSTU-10 primarily anchor to the oxygen atoms of the oxalate ligands, forming strong C-H···O interactions (2.701-2.987 Å). Additional weaker C-H···O interactions at around 3.933 Å are formed with distal oxygen atoms. Along the b-axis direction, C3H6 molecules interact with the triazole linkers via hydrogen-bonding interactions of d(C3H6···TRZ) C-N···H at around 2.477-2.980 Å. The static binding energy of C3H6 at the binding sites was calculated to be 41.4 kJ mol-1, which is in good agreement with the experimental Qst value (45.5 kJ mol-1). In comparison, the static binding energy of C3H8 was only 13.2 kJ mol-1, revealing much weaker binding forces. As depicted in Supplementary Fig. 62, C3H6 molecules located in the middle of the pore cavity in ZSTU-11, forming multiple C-H···O interactions (2.792-3.536 Å) and intermolecular d(C3H6···TRZ) C-H···N (2.999-3.246 Å) interactions with the framework. The calculated static binding energy for C3H6 in ZSTU-11 is 42.4 kJ mol-1, while the static binding energy for C3H8 is 20.3 kJ mol-1, with the latter being higher than in ZSTU-10 (Supplementary Figs. 61-62). Moreover, electrostatic potentials (ESP) of the pore structure of ZSTU-10, ZSTU-11, and ZSTU-12 were also calculated by DFT-D calculations, and the differentiated framework energy was exhibited in Supplementary Figs. 63-65 (the corresponding energy order is ZSTU-11 > ZSTU-10 > ZSTU-12). The results reveal strong negative potentials near the oxygen atoms of oxalate ligands. Simulated results and calculated static binding energies are consistent with the experimental sorption phenomenon of ZSTU-10 and ZSTU-11.

To obtain direct structural insight into the adsorption behavior of ZSTU-10, high-resolution neutron powder diffraction (NPD) experiments were conducted to accurately establish the supramolecular binding forces between C3D6 molecules and the framework (Supplementary Fig. 11b). Two independent adsorption sites (site Ι and Ⅱ) of C3D6 molecules were identified within the pore cavity constructed by four oxalate and eight triazole ligands, as shown in Figs. 4a-b and Supplementary Fig. 60). The occupancy of two C3D6 adsorption sites was refined to be 0.133 and 0.364 at sites Ι and Ⅱ, respectively, indicating that each unit cell can accommodate two C3D6 molecules. This result corresponds to a volumetric uptake of 101.0 cm3 cm-3 (STP), which is in excellent agreement with the experimental uptake from the C3H6 isotherm (97.3 cm3 cm-3) at 298 K and 1 bar. As depicted in Fig. 4, site Ⅱ serves as the predominant sorption site and owns a higher occupancy, which was anchored by the surrounding oxalate ligands to form multiple C-D···O interactions (2.386-3.402 Å). Site Ι is located adjacent to the oxalate ligands and triazole ligands, binding to these ligands via C-D···N interactions (2.048-3.361 Å) and stronger C-D···O (2.222-3.501 Å) hydrogen bonds (Fig. 4c). In addition, a negligible framework deformation can be found when comparing the structure of activated ZSTU-10 with that of C3D6-loaded ZSTU-10, confirming the structural rigidity of ZSTU-10. These results demonstrate that the precise pore window and expansive cavity are prerequisites for achieving effective molecular sieving and high-density C3H6 packing, while the interconnected diffusion channels are essential for facilitating rapid guest transport.

Breakthrough experiments
Motivated by the superior separation capacity of ZSTU-10 in single-component adsorption/desorption performance, we further conducted binary C3H6/C3H8 (v/v=50/50) column breakthrough experiments, in which equimolar binary mixtures flowed over the sample bed of MOFs with different flow rates at 298 K (Supplementary Fig. 66). Dynamic breakthrough experiments revealed that both ZSTU-10 and ZSTU-11 are capable of separating C3H6 from an equimolar C3H6/C3H8 mixtures (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Fig. 71). However, the separation efficiency distinguishes the two materials. Notably, at a total flow rate of 3 mL min-1, the breakthrough curves for the equimolar C3H6/C3H8 mixture show that C3H8 elutes first, and the co-adsorption interval is short (4.2 min g-1). After the overlap ends, a clear time window is observed in which C3H6 is retained while C3H8 has already eluted, enabling a wide separation window with mass-normalized retention time of approximately 16.6 min g-1 for high-purity C3H6 collection (Fig. 5a). The dynamic C3H6 capacity of ZSTU-10 was calculated to be 2.76 mmol g-1 based on C3H6/C3H8 breakthrough adsorption curves, surpassing that of ZU-609 (1.64 mmol g-1)60, KAUST-7 (0.65 mmol g-1)37, Y-abtc (1.26 mmol g-1)37 and Co-gallate (0.98 mmol g-1)38 (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 67). At a higher flow rate of 5 mL min-1, ZSTU-10 maintains a limited co-adsorption interval (8.6 min g-1), whereas ZSTU-11 exhibits a substantially longer co-adsorption interval (15 min g-1) under comparable conditions (Supplementary Figs. 68 and 72). Besides, the retention time of C3H6/C3H8 for ZSTU-11 below the co-adsorption interval reveals the poor separation efficiency. The shorter overlap for ZSTU-10 indicates reduced co-elution and thus improved dynamic separation performance for equimolar C3H6/C3H8 mixtures. The excellent breakthrough performance of ZSTU-10 prompted us to explore C3H6 purity and productivity, the desorption experiments were conducted through helium gas sweeping (10 mL min-1) at 448 K (Supplementary Fig. 69). Correspondingly, the purity and productivity of the preferentially adsorbed C3H6 was 99.1% and 37.5 L kg-1 (Figs. 5e-f and Supplementary Fig. 70). These metrics exceed those of reported benchmark MOFs with sensational performance, such as for KAUST-7 (16.3 L kg-1, 90% purity )46 and Y-abtc (1.3 L kg-1, 90% purity)37 (Supplementary Table 9). Five consecutive breakthrough adsorption/desorption measurements for an equimolar C3H6/C3H8 mixture were carried out at the flow rate of 5 mL min-1. The results revealed consistent retention times, no obvious loss of capacity, and a sustained C3H6 dynamic capture at around 3.7 mmol g-1 (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Fig. 68), confirming the excellent regenerability and cycling stability of ZSTU-10. Overall, these dynamic results demonstrate the practical potential of ZSTU-10 for C3H6/C3H8 separation. Because C3H8 adsorption is strongly suppressed by molecular sieving, regeneration primarily involves desorbing C3H6 from the high-affinity sites, which can reduce unnecessary energy expenditure associated with co-adsorbed impurities.

Given the demanding conditions prevalent in practical industrial production, we investigated the stability of ZSTU-10 under a range of relevant environments. The synthesized sample was exposed to air for 15 d and immersed in water for a week. The PXRD patterns indicate that ZSTU-10 can maintain substantial structural integrity without phase change or loss of crystallinity. Stable adsorption capacities of C3H6 for ZSTU-10 can be preserved after treatment with water at different time intervals (Supplementary Fig. 19). Furthermore, this material was soaked in different chemical environments for a week, such as organic solvents (DMF, MeOH, EtOH, CH2Cl2, ACN and acetone) and acid and alkaline solutions (pH = 2, 4, 10, 12). In all cases, the samples exhibited PXRD patterns identical to the simulated one, demonstrating exceptional chemical stability (Supplementary Figs. 20-21). Five consecutive single-component adsorption-desorption isotherms were conducted at 298 K and 1 bar, which consistently showed high levels of C3H6 adsorption capacity on ZSTU-10 (Fig. 5g and Supplementary Fig. 72). Additionally, the synthesis of ZSTU-10 uses inexpensive, readily available raw materials and demonstrates potential for scalability. Combined the advantages of good stability, low production cost, and the ability to simultaneously exclude C3H8 while efficiently adsorbing C3H6 renders ZSTU-10 a promising candidate for industrial application.

---

## Methods

Synthesis of ZSTU-10
ZnCO3 (0.627 g, 5 mmol), H2C2O4 (0.45 g, 5 mmol), and 1,2,4-triazole (TRZ, 1.727 g, 25 mmol) were added to the mixture of H2O (15 mL) and N-butyl alcohol (n-BuOH) (15 mL) in a 100 mL Teflon-lined reaction vessel. The mixed solution was stirred for an hour and reacted in an oven at 453 K for three days. After cooling to room temperature naturally, the resulting colorless crystals were collected by filtration and washed thoroughly with methanol. Finally, the product was dried in air overnight. To assess the potential for scale-up, we optimized the synthesis conditions. We confirmed that ZSTU-10 can be synthesized with high purity and crystallinity using a reduced molar ratio of 1:1:5, significantly lowering ligand consumption. Based on this optimized ratio and laboratory reagent prices, the estimated raw material cost is approximately $50.1 kg-1 (Supplementary Fig. 73), which serves as a promising baseline for future industrial economic evaluation.

Synthesis of ZSTU-11 and ZSTU-12
ZSTU-11 and ZSTU-12 were synthesized following the same procedure as ZSTU-10, except that n-BuOH was replaced by n-propyl alcohol (n-PrOH) or Isopropyl alcohol (i-PrOH), respectively.

Single-component sorption experiments
Prior to gas adsorption tests, approximately 200 mg of samples in the sample cell were activated under a dynamic vacuum at 423 K overnight to remove the guest molecules until the pressure stabilized. After each single-adsorption measurement, the sample cell was degassed at 333 K under vacuum for 0.5 h. C3H6 and C3H8 adsorption isotherms were collected from 243 K to 333 K on an automatic volumetric adsorption instrument (Micromeritics 3-Flex analyzer, 3-Flex Version 5.02). For each pressure point, an equilibrium time of 6 min was applied. Data were recorded only after a stability criterion was met: the system pressure changed by less than 0.1% over a consecutive 2 min period. The experimental adsorption-desorption temperatures were controlled by the ice bath (273 K) and a constant water bath (298 K). The Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) specific surface areas were analyzed using nitrogen adsorption isotherms at 77 K. The 195 K CO2 was performed in the mixtures of dry ice and acetone. The low temperatures from 243 K to 263 K were controlled by the mixtures of dry ice, ethanol, and ethylene glycol. The data visualization uses OriginPro 2024.

Dynamic breakthrough experiments
Fixed bed breakthrough experiments were carried out in a packed stainless steel column (10 mm × 12 cm) at 298 K and 1 bar. The breakthrough column was filled with activated samples (3.6 g) at ambient conditions. A stream of Argon was introduced into the column to purge the adsorbents for 15 h at 423 K in a temperature controller of the thermostat before the breakthrough experiments. The total inlet flow rate was controlled by calibrated mass flow controllers (MFCs) and was kept constant throughout each breakthrough experiment. The breakthrough column experiments were conducted using the gas mixture of C3H6/C3H8 (v/v, 50/50) with a stable flow rate of 5 mL min-1 at 298 K, and the outgas of the column was monitored by a gas chromatograph (GC-2014C Shimadzu) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector for continuous gas analysis. When both C3H6 and C3H8 reached equilibrium, the desorption experiments were conducted through high-purity Ar (99.999%) with a flow rate of 10 mL min-1 at 298 K, and then heated up to 448 K to sweep. Five consecutive breakthrough adsorption–desorption cycles were performed to evaluate the cycling stability of ZSTU-10.
